summary: A student who thinks all bonding is electron sharing works through the transfer-versus-sharing distinction using sodium chloride and water.
student_turns: I'm doing bonding for my chemistry mock and I keep mixing up ionic and covalent, can you help me sort it out?
I thought both types were basically atoms sharing electrons so everyone ends up with a full outer shell?
So in sodium chloride, is it the sodium and the chlorine sharing an electron so they both get to 8?
Wait, so the electron actually moves from sodium to chlorine and doesn't come back? That's not the same as water then?
But if sodium loses an electron doesn't that mean its outer shell isn't full anymore, so why does that make it stable?

text: Rates of reaction and collision theory
summary: A discouraged student who keeps losing marks on rates of reaction questions works toward a full collision-theory explanation.
student_turns: I always lose marks on the rates of reaction questions and I don't get why, it's actually so annoying.
It's usually the ones asking why increasing the concentration speeds up the reaction.
I just write 'there's more particles so it reacts faster' but that never gets full marks.
Is it something to do with the particles bumping into each other more often?
So how do I actually turn that into a proper 6-mark answer without just saying the same sentence three times?

summary: An exam-preparation session linking the acid–alkali titration required practical to mole and concentration calculations.
student_turns: My chemistry exam's coming up and I want to go over the titration required practical because I always get muddled with the calculations after it.
I remember using a pipette to measure the alkali into the conical flask and adding the acid from the burette until the indicator changed colour.
Why do we do a rough titration first and then repeat it until we get concordant results?
If I know the volume and concentration of the acid I used, how do I work out how many moles of it reacted?
Once I've got the moles of acid, how do I actually use that to find the concentration of the alkali?
